title: CSQ Unit 7 · Make Your Own Game (6-8)

items.q: A plan of who does what by when, for a team project, is a…
Breaking a game into "menu", "play loop", "scoring" before building is…
Your team has 3 sessions and 4 features. You should…
choices: build everything at the same time
set milestones and split the features
let one person do it all
items.why: Milestones split the work across the sessions and say who builds which feature by when, so the team can tick off progress and finish on time.

choices: "the whole game, built all at once"
start screen · play loop · scoring · end screen
"make it fun, make it cool, make it big"
items.why: Decomposition breaks the game into parts that can each be built and tested on their own: start screen, play loop, scoring and end screen.

items.q: A 6-box flowchart of your game's main rule helps because…
choices: it shows the decisions before you build
it is prettier than a list
items.why: A flowchart draws each step as a box and each decision as a diamond. Drawing the rule first shows whether it is clear before you spend time building.

items.q: A table of input, expected, actual and pass/fail is a…
Why write test cases before you test?
choices: so you check what matters, not just what you notice
to use up more of the messages
so the Builder gets a rest between them
items.why: Test cases written ahead make you check the parts that matter, including edges like zero lives or the last second, not just whatever you happen to notice.

items.q: The score goes up when you lose a life. Which message is best?
choices: "Expected the score to stay the same when a life is lost; it goes up by 1. Fix that."
items.why: A precise fix names the situation, what you expected and what actually happened. That tells the Builder exactly which rule to change.

items.q: Which is a good range of test cases for a timer?
choices: start, halfway, and the last second
items.why: Testing the start, the middle and the very last second covers the timer's whole range, including the edge where bugs often hide.

items.q: Changing your game because of what players said is…
Feedback from many testers helps because…
choices: one tester's opinion is always enough
it is faster than testing it yourself
items.why: One tester is a story, and many testers are data. Different players run into different problems, so more testers find more of them.

items.q: 7 of 9 testers rated level 2 "too hard". Which change does the data support?
choices: make level 2 easier, then test again
change the title of the game
items.why: Most testers found level 2 too hard, so the data points at level 2. Make it easier, then test again to check that the change worked.

items.q: Pooling every team's tally sheets is an example of…
items.why: Crowdsourcing means collecting input from many people. Pooling every team's tallies gathers feedback from the whole class at once.

items.q: A "How to play" card and a "How it works" note are…
Documentation makes a program easier to…
items.why: Documentation explains how the program works, so someone else can follow it, test it and find the bugs in it.

items.q: Which "How it works" line is most useful?
choices: "score goes up by 10 per star; lives at 0 ends the game"
items.why: This line names the real rules: how the score changes and what ends the game. A classmate could use it to test or change the game.

items.q: Credits in your game should name…
choices: the template, art and ideas you reused
items.why: Credits name everything you reused, like the template, the art and other people's ideas, written the way each license asks.
